Key ideas

Analysing decay series diagrams

Definitions

Radioactive decay series: the sequence of stages a radioisotope passes through to become more stable. The chain ends when a stable isotope forms.
Parent nucleus: the decaying nucleus
Daughter nucleus: a nucleus formed by the radioactive decay of another nucleus (the parent)
Decay chain: the sequence of stages a radioisotope passes through until it reaches a stable nucleus

Formulas

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, 3D glossary and formula boxes2
3D

New knowledgeRadioactive decay series

Analysing decay series diagrams

The naturally occurring radioactive isotopes of the heaviest elements fall into chains of successive disintegrations, or decays, and all the species in one chain constitute a radioactive family, or radioactive decay series.

Three of these series include most of the naturally radioactive elements of the periodic table.

They are the uranium series, the actinium series and the thorium series.

Each series is characterised by a parent (first member) that has a long half-life and a series of daughter nuclides that ultimately lead to a stable end-product – that is, a nuclide on the band of stability.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 423
3D

New knowledgeRadioactive decay series

Analysing decay series diagrams

In all three series, the end-product is a stable isotope of lead.

NOTE: The neptunium series is a fourth series.

However, since neptunium-237 has a relatively short half-life (21 million years), neptunium-237 is no longer present in the crust of Earth but the rest of its decay series is still present and continuing to decay.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 424
3D

New knowledgeThe decay chain of uranium-238

Analysing decay series diagrams

A parent nucleus of uranium-238 decays by alpha emission to form a daughter nucleus, thorium-234.

The thorium produced in turn undergoes β−β^{-}β−-decay and transforms into protactinium-234, which then undergoes β−β^{-}β−-decay to produce uranium-234.

This last isotope changes slowly by alpha decay (with a half-life of 245 000 years) into thorium-230, yet another unstable nucleus and so on.

Any such decay chain is only stopped by the formation of a stable nucleus.

Figure 3D–2 The uranium-238 decay series. The half-life and emission type are indicated on each of the decays as the radioactive uranium-238 is eventually transformed into stable element lead-206.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 435
3D

New knowledgeThe decay chain of uranium-238

Analysing decay series diagrams

This occurs at the 14th generation of the uranium-238 family, when lead 206 is finally produced (Figure 3D–2).

Note that the daughters of α-decay shown in Figure 3D–2 always have two fewer protons and two fewer neutrons than the parent.

Therefore, uranium-238 under α-decay becomes thorium-234.

Note that the daughter thorium-234 produced has two fewer protons and four fewer nucleons than the parent uranium-238: 92238U→90234Th+24He^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}92238​U→90234​Th+24​He The daughters of β-decay have one fewer neutron and one more proton than their parent.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 436
3D

New knowledgeThe decay chain of uranium-238

Analysing decay series diagrams

Beta decay therefore produces daughter nuclei that move up the periodic table.

Therefore, a thorium-234 nucleus beta decays to protactinium-234 and in turn protactinium-234, which is also a β-emitter, produces uranium-234. 90234Th→91234Pa+−10β^{234}_{90}\text{Th} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta90234​Th→91234​Pa+−10​β 91234Pa→92234U+−10β^{234}_{91}\text{Pa} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{0}_{-1}\beta91234​Pa→92234​U+−10​β It was noted earlier that α-decay and β-decay are often associated with subsequent γ-decays (Section 3B).

For example, in the α-decay of U-238, two γ-rays of different energies are emitted in addition to the α-particle: 92238U→90234Th+24He+2 00γ^{238}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} + 2\,{}^{0}_{0}\gamma92238​U→90234​Th+24​He+200​γ No γ-decays are shown in the chart in Figure 3D–2, because they do not produce a daughter nucleus that differs from the parent nucleus.

For example, an excited magnesium-24 nucleus (with the asterisk * indicating an excited nucleus) emits a γ-ray but still remains a magnesium-24 nucleus: 1224Mg∗→1224Mg+00γ^{24}_{12}\text{Mg}^{*} \rightarrow {}^{24}_{12}\text{Mg} + {}^{0}_{0}\gamma1224​Mg∗→1224​Mg+00​γ Not all naturally occurring radioisotopes are part of a decay series.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 437
3D

New knowledgeThe decay chain of uranium-238

Analysing decay series diagrams

For example, the potassium-40 found on Earth is a remnant of the supernova explosion that created Earth.

The half-life of 1.25 billion years is so long that these radioisotopes are still decaying from when they were formed.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 3, p. 438
